claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its simple solid-solution state.
The low hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi are governed by the absence of nanoscale secondary-phase precipitates or local chemical inhomogeneities.
Nanoscale precipitates or local chemical inhomogeneities enhance dislocation pinning and lattice-distortion strengthening.
The favorable plasticity and machinability of homogeneous CoCrFeNiTi arise from relatively unimpeded dislocation motion.
The starting alloy is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi and is a single-phase solid solution without intentionally induced precipitates or chemical clustering.
A minor alloying addition or heat treatment can be used to promote nanoscale precipitates or chemical clustering in CoCrFeNiTi.
The relevant structural comparison is the presence after intervention versus absence before intervention of nanoscale precipitates or clusters.
Nanoscale precipitates or clusters act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Unmodified CoCrFeNiTi has only modest solid-solution strengthening because it has low lattice distortion.
The lack of precipitates permits relatively free dislocation motion, producing high ductility but low hardness and strength.
Introducing nanoscale precipitates or chemical inhomogeneities will raise yield strength and hardness through precipitation strengthening.
Precipitation strengthening will likely reduce plasticity.
Relative to baseline CoCrFeNiTi, precipitate-containing samples will have increased hardness and yield strength.
Relative to baseline CoCrFeNiTi, precipitate-containing samples will have reduced ductility.
The homogeneous baseline has relatively low hardness and yield strength but superior plasticity and machinability.
The hypothesis applies under quasi-static loading from approximately 25 °C to 600 °C.
The hypothesis may not hold when twinning or phase transformations dominate or at extreme loading rates.
The magnitude of strengthening and the strength-ductility balance depend on precipitate type, size, distribution, and volume fraction.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing a homogeneous control with an otherwise matched precipitate-induced sample using microscopy, hardness, strength, and plastic-strain measurements.
Failure to increase hardness and yield strength, or strengthening without reduced ductility, would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says reduced plasticity is only likely, and the uncertainty field says the strength-ductility balance may vary with precipitate type, but the falsification rule treats strengthening without reduced ductility as decisive falsification.

The experiment permits either heat treatment or a minor alloying addition while requiring all other parameters to be identical. An alloying addition changes composition and is therefore not a clean single-variable comparison with the equimolar baseline unless a separate composition-matched control is defined.
